skills.when_to_use: Use when the question demands precise cross-video correspondence, discrimination, or selection among videos/options, recognizable from the question text and video list alone: questions about visually labeled object IDs across synchronized camera views, including where one object is when an event involving another occurs, an object's trajectory or final motion, or where an object sits in the frame when another leaves a view; questions that name a time interval or timestamp in one video and ask for the functionally equivalent step or interval in another, or otherwise require a time-interval answer about a specific visible action; questions asking which of several videos, segments, or options exhibits a stated property, state, error, or ending condition (for example, which one ends with the protagonist in a stated situation); or questions asking which action is performed incorrectly a stated number of times across videos of the same activity. Do not use for open narrative inference questions (e.g., predicting a middle segment from a beginning and an ending) where summarizing each video separately suffices.
skills.strategy: Apply this procedure in order; it overrides the default single-pass workflow. Stage 1, adaptive first acquisition. For synchronized multi-view questions with labeled object IDs, the question text states each ID is shown with a colored box during its first visible second: include that fact in every instruction you issue, and ask the analyst or visual model to scan the opening seconds for that box to initialize identity before tracking. When the question hinges on a synchronized moment or cross-view comparison (e.g., where object B is when event A occurs in the other view), you may open with a single joint watch over short synchronized windows instead of per-video analyses, because per-video agents cannot exploit time synchronization; use per-video analysis first only when the needed facts are view-local (e.g., an object's own trajectory within its view). For all other questions, issue one per-video instruction per referenced video asking for a timestamped, purely descriptive account of the relevant objects, actions, or scenes, with a complete timeline of every occurrence of the target action across the whole video, not just the first instance. Never embed answer options, a yes/no verdict request, or an expected conclusion in a first pass; for property-selection questions, ask for raw descriptions of the relevant moments and decide the property yourself from those details. For a referenced event at a stated time, request that interval plus several seconds of context. Stage 2, consistency gate before answering. Raise a flag when: (a) two reports about the same object or moment directly conflict, including a later report locating an object an earlier report called not visible; (b) a referenced labeled object is reported not visible or unidentifiable, since these questions presuppose it appears; (c) a report is degenerate relative to the required answer, such as a single point timestamp where an interval is required, an event anchored at exactly 0.0 seconds or at a selected clip's boundary, or an action with no visible duration; (d) a report's raw visual description contradicts its own interpretive conclusion; (e) a candidate interval came from a watch whose total selected duration was long relative to the detail sought; (f) an acquired observation (e.g., a described relative position or direction) matches none of the answer options, or the only support for a chosen option is an inference about what the question must have meant rather than a described visual fact. Stage 3, re-acquisition until flags resolve. Do not answer from flagged evidence and do not guess from assumptions about how question sets are constructed. Re-acquisition is not capped at one attempt: while decision steps remain and a flag persists, run another focused follow-up and vary the method when the previous one failed. If per-video analyses could not find a labeled object, switch to a joint watch of the relevant views over the window where it should appear (its labeled first second or the claimed event moment), with the colored-box initialization context stated. If a joint watch returned a degenerate anchor or an option-mismatching fact, re-watch a shorter, denser window around the claimed moment, or fall back to per-video instructions carrying the colored-box context, asking for raw layout only. For identity or position conflicts across synchronized views, use a joint watch clipped to a short window around the claimed moment and ask for the raw visual layout without stating which option is correct. For any time-interval answer, before submitting it run one dense confirmation watch on a tight window covering the candidate interval plus a few seconds before and after, asking for the action's full visible start and end seconds and whether it recurs elsewhere; adjust or reject the candidate accordingly. Stage 4, final answer from raw description. Answer only from described visual content, not from an analyst's or visual model's verdict phrase and not from plausibility priors about intended answers. If the question presupposes exactly one correct option but raw descriptions still fail to support any option after re-acquisition is exhausted, choose the option whose support rests on the strongest described visual details, re-read the raw descriptions for a resolving detail, and record residual uncertainty in the reason. Never select an option by reasoning that the evidence must be wrong, and never substitute a discussion of missing evidence for the requested answer representation.
